questions.question: What are the three roles of `iter()`, `next()`, and `StopIteration` in Python's iterator protocol?
options: `iter()` sorts, `next()` filters, `StopIteration` resets the iterator
`iter()` returns an iterator object, `next()` pulls the next item, `StopIteration` signals the end
`iter()` counts elements, `next()` skips to the last item, `StopIteration` raises an error permanently
`iter()` creates a list, `next()` appends to it, `StopIteration` converts it to a tuple
questions.explanation: `iter(obj)` returns an iterator (an object with a `__next__` method). `next(it)` retrieves the next value. When no items remain, `StopIteration` is raised, signalling the `for` loop or comprehension to stop.

questions.question: What is the primary memory advantage of a generator over a list?
options: Generators are always faster to iterate
Generators produce values one at a time on demand, so they do not hold the full sequence in memory
Generators can store more data types than lists
Generators are automatically cached to disk
questions.explanation: A list materialises all elements in memory at once. A generator yields values lazily — only computing each item when `next()` is called. This makes generators ideal for large datasets like reading millions of log records without running out of RAM.

questions.question: What keyword turns a regular function into a generator function?
options: return
async
yield
iter
questions.explanation: Any function containing a `yield` statement is a generator function. Calling it returns a generator object. Each `yield` suspends the function, saves its state, and delivers a value. The function resumes from where it paused on the next `next()` call.

questions.question: What does `yield from sub_generator` do?
options: Creates a copy of sub_generator
Converts sub_generator into a list
Delegates iteration to sub_generator, transparently forwarding each of its yielded values
Runs sub_generator in a separate thread
questions.explanation: `yield from` delegates to another iterable or generator, yielding each of its values in turn. It is equivalent to a `for item in sub_generator: yield item` loop but more efficient and supports two-way communication via `.send()`.

questions.question: A data pipeline processes 10 million transaction records from a CSV. Which approach is most memory-efficient?
options: Read all rows into a list with `list(csv_reader)`, then process the list
Use a generator that yields one parsed row at a time
Load the CSV into a dictionary
Split the CSV into 1000 smaller files first
questions.explanation: Loading 10 million rows into a list could consume gigabytes of RAM. A generator that reads and yields one row at a time keeps memory usage constant regardless of file size — only one row exists in memory at each step.
